AuthResponse.description:
The answer to "send me a code" and to "set my password".

Deliberately carries **no token**. It used to have
``access_token: str | None = None``, which nothing ever populated —
zero call sites — and that is worse than it sounds rather than
harmless.

These are the responses to requests made by an anonymous caller who
has typed in an email address. ``services/email/delivery.py`` explains
why handing anything back is the wrong shape: "returning the code in
the response would let anyone request one for any address and read it
straight back — account takeover, dressed as a convenience feature."
A nullable ``access_token`` sitting on exactly that response is a
field pre-shaped for that mistake, waiting for somebody to fill it in
the week a user complains about an extra step.

Signing in really does return a token, from ``/sign-in``,
``/sign-in-with-code`` and ``/sign-up`` — those answer with
``TokenResponse``, which is where a token belongs.

constraints. A caller that already has this response has the token
in a POST body, which is where a credential belongs. The **browser**
doing the desktop handoff has to get it to a local HTTP server by
navigating there, and a token in a navigation lands in history.

So the browser gets `handoff_code` — the same single-use,
30-second, `GETDEL`-redeemed code F107 built for the sign-in
redirect — and exchanges it at `POST /v1/auth/exchange`. F124.

get.description:
Liveness: this process is running and serving.

Deliberately checks nothing. A liveness probe that fails when the
database is unreachable gets the container killed and restarted for a
problem a restart cannot fix, turning a database blip into a restart
loop. Use ``/ready`` to decide whether to send traffic.

Readiness: this process can actually serve a request.

503 when a dependency is down, so an orchestrator can drain the
instance without killing it. The checks are the cheapest possible
round trip to each — ``SELECT 1`` and a ``PING`` — because this
endpoint gets polled.

**A busy pool is not an unready process.** The check shares the
application's connection pool, so it cannot be insulated from the
exhaustion it exists to detect; but under a burst it would then queue,
time out and get the pod pulled out of service, sending its traffic to
a sibling replica that saturates in turn.

So saturation and unavailability are answered differently. The check
waits a short, fixed time; if it does not get a connection and the
pool is full, that is ``busy`` and the process stays **ready**,
because removing a working replica from a load balancer is the one
action guaranteed to make a capacity problem worse. Anything else —
the server refusing, the host unreachable, a timeout with the pool
*not* full — is ``unavailable``, and that is a 503. F116.
